levels.title: Plan the Route
levels.story: Dara hands Kit a slip: "Fetch every crate heavier than 40 kilos from Quay 3." Clerk Cobb in the Route Office taps it. "Writing the request is the easy part," he says. "Deciding the route is the real work."

everyday.scene: You ask a map app for the way to a friend's house. It does not just draw any road. It tries several routes, guesses how long each will take, and shows you the quickest.
everyday.question: What does a database do when you send it a question in SQL?
everyday.answer: SQL says what you want, not how to get it. The database checks the question, works out several ways to answer it, estimates what each costs, and runs the cheapest.

lessons.title: From SQL to rows
text: A query passes through stages. The parser checks the syntax and builds a query tree. The rewriter applies stored rules, such as expanding a view. The planner creates a plan. The executor runs that plan and hands back the rows.
You write what you want. The database decides how. Every query you send passes through these stages, in this order. They are PostgreSQL's names for them.

terms.meaning: The chosen list of steps the database will run.
The stage that chooses the plan.

references.title: PostgreSQL documentation: The Path of a Query

lessons.title: Many ways, one plan
text: The planner builds the possible paths that give the same result. If a table has an index, one path scans the whole table and another uses the index. It estimates the cost of each path and keeps the cheapest.
Those estimates come from statistics about the data, which are only samples. So a plan is only as good as its guesses.

predict.prompt: Path A costs 700, path B costs 450 and path C costs 520. Which one does the planner choose?
predict.answer: Path B, because it has the lowest estimated cost.

references.title: PostgreSQL documentation: The Path of a Query

lessons.title: Reading a plan
text: Databases will show you the plan. PostgreSQL uses EXPLAIN and SQLite uses EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. The table below is real SQLite output for a table of 200 parcels.

SCAN means every row is looked at. SEARCH means the database jumps to the rows it needs, using an index or the primary key. After the index idx_w was created, the same question changed from SCAN to SEARCH.

feed.answer: SEARCH, using the index. Without the index it would say SCAN.

fieldNotes.title: The planner shows its work
fieldNotes.text: PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN command shows the plan the planner chose, with its cost estimates, without you changing the query.

fieldNotes.title: Plans change with indexes
fieldNotes.text: In SQLite, adding an index can change the plan for the same query from SCAN to SEARCH.

summary: You followed a query through the parser, the rewriter, the planner and the executor, saw why the planner estimates costs, and read real SCAN and SEARCH plan lines.
Cobb stamps the slip. "Choose the route first, then walk it."

mistake.title: Thinking the database runs your SQL line by line
mistake.text: SQL describes the result you want. The planner chooses the steps, and the executor runs them. The steps can change when an index is added, even if your SQL does not.

levels.title: Cost of a Crossing
levels.story: Cobb points at two quays. "Quay A holds 40 crates of manifests. Quay B holds 200 crates of cargo. To match each manifest line to its cargo, I could walk all of B for every single line. Or I could be smarter."

everyday.scene: You have a list of 40 guests and a box of 200 name tags. You could look through the whole box for every guest. Or you could pin the tags into alphabetical pigeonholes first and go straight to the right one.
everyday.question: How does the effort change as the lists grow?
everyday.answer: Checking every tag for every guest multiplies the two sizes. Smarter methods, like pigeonholes, touch each list about once.

lessons.title: Cost is counting pages
text: A plan's cost is a score, mostly counting page reads. PostgreSQL scores a full table scan as pages x seq_page_cost, plus rows x cpu_tuple_cost. By default those two settings are 1.0 and 0.01.
A table of 500 pages and 20,000 rows scores 500 + 200 = 700. A page fetched out of order scores more: random_page_cost is 4.0 by default, so 100 scattered pages score 400.

terms.meaning: A score for a plan, mostly counting page reads.

lessons.title: Nested loops
text: A nested loop join takes each row of the outer table R and scans the inner table S for matches. Read cost: pages of R, plus rows of R times pages of S. A block version loads a chunk of R into memory and scans S once per chunk. Here a chunk is one page of R.
With R of 40 pages and 1,000 rows, and S of 200 pages, the two costs are in the table.

terms.meaning: The table whose rows drive the loop.
The table scanned again for each row or chunk.

head: Method
Page reads
Total
rows: A page of R at a time

lessons.title: Hash join
text: A hash join reads the smaller table into a hash table in memory, then reads the other table once and looks each row up. If the hash table fits in memory, each table is read once: 40 + 200 = 240 page reads here.
It needs an equality join, one that uses =. Typically it beats nested loops, except when the probe side is very small.

text.text: If the hash table does not fit in memory, the Grace hash join first splits both tables into partitions with a hash function and writes them out to disk. It then loads each matching pair of partitions into memory, builds a hash table for the smaller one and looks up the other.

feed.explain: Pages read from storage are the main cost.

feed.prompt: In a nested loop join, which table is scanned again for each row or chunk?

feed.prompt: A table has 300 pages and 12,000 rows. With the default settings, what is the scan cost?

fieldNotes.title: Cost settings
fieldNotes.text: PostgreSQL's planner scores a page read in order as 1.0 by default and a page read out of order as 4.0.

fieldNotes.title: Hash joins
fieldNotes.text: A hash join builds hash tables from the tuples of one or both tables, and then probes them. It needs an equality condition.

summary: You counted page reads to cost a table scan, compared row-by-row and page-by-page nested loops, and saw a hash join read each table once.
Cobb nods at the hash table. "Build once, look up many."

mistake.title: Comparing joins by the number of rows alone
mistake.text: Cost is about page reads, and the way the tables are visited matters. The same join can need 200,040 page reads or 240, depending on the method.
